newsitem.title: USA: Indiana high court hears property assessment case.
newsitem.headline: Indiana high court hears property assessment case.

text.p: Indiana Supreme Court late Thursday heard oral arguments in a lawsuit challenging the state's method of assessing property taxes.
The state had appealed a May 31 ruling by Indiana Tax Court that found the assessment system to be unconstitutional.

John Laramore, a deputy Indiana attorney general, said Friday the state argued the current system is legal because "the state constitution gives the legislature the freedom to require a number of valuations in addition to market value."
He said that if the current system is unconstitutional, the state would be barred from offering special tax treatments, such as a homestead exemption.
The tax court had given the state until March 1, 1998, to fix the current assessment system, which relies largely on calculating the replacement value of property.
Laramore said the court made it clear it would expedite a decision in the case.
Indiana's Legislature is expected to take up the assessment issue when it convenes in January.

A lawyer from the Indiana Civil Liberties Union, which is representing taxpayers and a town in northwest Indiana that filed the lawsuit against the Indiana Board of Tax Commissioners, was not available to comment.
The group had successfully argued before the tax court that the current assessment system results in inequities of taxes paid.
